title: Malachi 1:6–14
context: The LORD of Armies confronts the priests who despise his name. He states the charge; they reply, “How have we despised your name?” and “How have we polluted you?”; and he answers that they offer blind, lame, and sick animals and call his table contemptible (1:6–8, 12–13). He would rather the temple doors be shut than receive such worship (1:10), for his name is great among the nations (1:11, 14). Readers in both traditions take 1:11 as foreseeing worship among the Gentiles through the gospel, or as describing God’s name honored among the nations in Malachi’s day; these readings are held with care.

verses.text: “A son honors his father, and a servant his master. If I am a father, then where is my honor? And if I am a master, where is the respect due me?” says the LORD of Armies to you priests who despise my name. “You say, ‘How have we despised your name?’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “A son honors his father, and a servant his master. If I am a father, then where is my honor?” The priests reply, “How have we despised your name?” Arminian readers see leaders called to account.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD confronting priests who despise his name. Shared ground: God is both Father and Master, and those who serve at his altar owe him honor and reverence.

verses.text: You offer polluted bread on my altar. You say, ‘How have we polluted you?’ In that you say, ‘The LORD’s table is contemptible.’
verses.arminianNotes: “You offer polluted bread on my altar.” The priests ask, “How have we polluted you?” Arminian readers see the LORD answering that their contempt shows in calling his table contemptible.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see contempt for God shown in careless worship. Readers in this tradition note that the disputation pattern, statement, question, and answer, exposes attitudes the priests did not admit.

verses.text: When you offer the blind for sacrifice, isn’t that evil? And when you offer the lame and sick, isn’t that evil? Present it now to your governor! Will he be pleased with you? Or will he accept your person?” says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: “When you offer the blind for sacrifice, isn’t that evil? … Present it now to your governor!” Arminian readers see worship offered with less respect than a human ruler would receive.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the law’s ban on defective sacrifices broken (Deuteronomy 15:21). Shared ground: God deserves our best, and giving him leftovers reveals what we truly value.

verses.text: “Now, please entreat the favor of God, that he may be gracious to us. With this, will he accept any of you?” says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: “Now, please entreat the favor of God, that he may be gracious to us. With this, will he accept any of you?” Arminian readers hear irony: prayer cannot cover contempt shown in the offerings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear irony in the call to seek God’s favor while offering him defective gifts. Readers in this tradition see that true worship and genuine prayer go together.

verses.text: “Oh that there were one among you who would shut the doors, that you might not kindle fire on my altar in vain! I have no pleasure in you,” says the LORD of Armies, “neither will I accept an offering at your hand.
verses.arminianNotes: “Oh that there were one among you who would shut the doors, that you might not kindle fire on my altar in vain!” Arminian readers see the LORD preferring no worship to hypocritical worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God refusing offerings from those who despise him. Shared ground: outward ritual without reverence is worthless, and the LORD says, “I have no pleasure in you.”

verses.text: For from the rising of the sun even to its going down, my name is great among the nations, and in every place incense will be offered to my name, and a pure offering; for my name is great among the nations,” says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: “from the rising of the sun even to its going down, my name is great among the nations.” Arminian readers often hear a future worship of God among the Gentiles, fulfilled through the gospel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise often hear the worldwide worship of the church foretold. Others read it as God’s name honored among the nations in Malachi’s own day; readers in both traditions hold these readings with care.

verses.text: “But you profane it when you say, ‘The LORD’s table is polluted, and its fruit, even its food, is contemptible.’
verses.arminianNotes: “But you profane it when you say, ‘The LORD’s table is polluted, and its fruit, even its food, is contemptible.’” Arminian readers see the contrast between the nations honoring God’s name and the priests profaning it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the scandal of priests treating holy things as contemptible. Readers in this tradition note how sharply 1:11 and 1:12 are set side by side.

verses.text: You say also, ‘Behold, what a weariness it is!’ And you have sniffed at it”, says the LORD of Armies; “and you have brought that which was taken by violence, the lame, and the sick; thus you bring the offering. Should I accept this at your hand?” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “You say also, ‘Behold, what a weariness it is!’ And you have sniffed at it.” Arminian readers see weariness and disdain in worship, leading to stolen, lame, and sick offerings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see boredom with God’s service exposed. Shared ground: worship that becomes a burden to be endured rather than a joy reveals a heart that has drifted from God.

verses.text: “But the deceiver is cursed who has in his flock a male, and vows and sacrifices to the Lord a defective thing; for I am a great King,” says the LORD of Armies, “and my name is awesome among the nations.”
verses.arminianNotes: “But the deceiver is cursed who has in his flock a male, and vows and sacrifices to the Lord a defective thing; for I am a great King.” Arminian readers see deceit in withholding the best that was vowed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s kingship as the reason for reverent worship. The LORD declares, “my name is awesome among the nations,” and readers in this tradition see the chapter closing on his greatness.
